lead: Python code can be fed to the interpreter in two ways. In interactive mode you type one line at the >>> prompt and the answer appears at once. In script mode you save many lines in a file, such as area.py, and run the file with python area.py. Both use the same interpreter and the same rules. The practical difference is memory: an interactive answer disappears when you exit, while a saved script keeps the steps for tomorrow.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for a first program to run.

sections.h3: Two ways to feed the interpreter

blocks.text: A Python interpreter is the program that reads Python code and carries out its instructions. You can give it code in two ways. Interactive mode feeds one line at a time and answers at once. Script mode feeds a whole file, saved with a name such as area.py. The interpreter is the same in both modes; only the source of the lines changes.

Interactive mode is also called the REPL: Read, Evaluate, Print, Loop. It reads one line, evaluates it, prints a result when there is one, and loops back for the next line. The prompt >>> marks where you type. Script mode has no >>> prompt in the file. The file is plain text, and the command python area.py asks the interpreter to run it.

The choice is about what must survive. A quick test of one expression belongs at the prompt. A calculation you must repeat tomorrow belongs in a saved file. IDLE is one editor that can open both a shell and a file; it is not a third mode.

Start Python with no file name: python or python3. The screen shows a prompt >>>. Type 12 * 8 and press Enter. The interpreter evaluates the multiplication and prints 96 on the next line. A new >>> prompt appears. That is one turn of the REPL.

An expression typed at the prompt is printed automatically. An assignment such as x = 12 prints nothing, because the job is to store the name, not to show a value. After the assignment, typing x * 8 prints 96. The name x lives in that session only. Closing the session, by exit() or the keyboard end-of-file key, clears it.

Interactive mode is good for small checks: a unit conversion, a slice of a string, a doubt about operator order. It is poor for a long program, because the lines are not saved by default. A new session starts with no names from the old session. Use it as a scratch pad, not as a notebook unless you save the text yourself.

Script mode starts with a file. Open an editor, type the program, and save it with a .py ending, for example area.py. Put one instruction on each line. This file is the source code. The file can be opened, changed, copied and run again.

Run the file from a terminal in the folder that contains it: python area.py. On some systems the command is python3 area.py or py area.py. The interpreter reads the file from top to bottom, executes each line, and sends any print output to the screen. When the last line finishes, the program ends and its names are gone from memory.

The file survives. Running python area.py again repeats the same steps. That is the reason to use script mode for homework, lab records and real programs. If the interpreter reports an error, it gives a line number and a message; reading those is the first step of debugging. Full error families are in 1.8.

examples.question: A student wants the value of 12 × 8. First the student types 12 * 8 at the interactive prompt and sees an answer. Then the student writes print(12 * 8) in a file area.py and runs python area.py. What number appears on screen in each case? After the interactive session is closed, does the value 96 remain available to a new session? Give the final numeric output.
steps: Interactive step: at the >>> prompt type 12 * 8. The interpreter evaluates 12 × 8 = 96 and prints 96.
Exit the interactive session. The session memory is cleared. A new session starts empty, so the value 96 is not available.
Script step: the file area.py contains print(12 * 8). Run python area.py.
The interpreter reads the file top to bottom. It evaluates 12 × 8 = 96, and print sends 96 to the screen.
The file remains saved. Running python area.py again repeats the same output 96.
examples.answer: Both modes show 96; the saved script can repeat it, but the interactive value does not survive exit.

traps: A name typed at the prompt is still there tomorrow. A new session starts with an empty namespace; only a saved script repeats the steps.
Typing print(12 * 8) at the prompt and expecting silence. It prints 96; the expression 12 * 8 also prints 96 because the REPL prints expression values.
Saving the file but running the wrong command, such as typing only area.py in some shells. Use python area.py from the folder that holds the file.
Calling IDLE a third mode. IDLE is an editor and a shell; the two modes are interactive and script.
Forgetting that a script runs top to bottom. A line below a failed line may not run; read the reported line number first, then see 1.8.

quiz.q: Which prompt marks interactive mode in Python?
Why does a value typed in interactive mode not exist in a new session?
quiz.a: It is held only in the memory of the old interpreter session; no saved file stores it.

quiz.q: In a script, what does print(7 * 6) print?
At the prompt you type x = 5, then x + 3. What appears on screen for each line?
A student types result = 12 * 8 at the prompt, closes Python, opens a new prompt and types result. Explain the outcome.
quiz.a: The new session has an empty namespace, so result is not defined; Python raises a NameError. The old value 96 was not saved.

quiz.q: A lab needs the same 12 × 8 calculation every week. Compare interactive and script mode for this task.
quiz.a: Interactive mode gives 96 once but the line is not kept unless copied; a new session is empty. Script mode keeps print(12 * 8) in a file, so python area.py repeats 96 each week. Script mode is correct for repetition.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real Python work often uses an interactive notebook or a debugger console beside saved files; the same split between a quick probe and a kept script appears in data science. Production teams run saved scripts through version control and continuous integration, not by retyping lines. Search for Python REPL, notebook cells and python -i if you want to see how the idea grows.
